blocks.text: 1. Embedding Models
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447161018-665709857.png
Embedding models are the specific systems used to produce the vectors discussed so far, moving from theory to real tooling.
This topic surveys how real, deployed models actually generate those embeddings in practice.
2. From Concept To Concrete Model
Every embedding discussed so far had to come from some actual, trained model, as introduced in What are Embeddings.
This topic surveys the real options available for that role.
3. Open Versus Closed Models
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447161503-134314997.png
Some embedding models run locally as open weights, while others run only behind a hosted API.
That distinction shapes cost, latency, and data privacy tradeoffs.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Model type","Tradeoff"],"rows":[["Open weight, self hosted","Full data control, requires own infrastructure"],["Hosted API","Simple to use, data leaves your infrastructure per call"]]}

blocks.text: 4. General Purpose Versus Domain Specific
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447161505-845306434.png
A general purpose model trains on broad, varied text, while a domain specific model trains on a narrower, specialized corpus.
A legal or medical domain model often outperforms a general model on that specific domain.
5. Model Size And Quality
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447161505-30970930.png
A larger embedding model tends to capture richer, more nuanced meaning.
As with the cost of density covered in Dense Embeddings, that richer meaning comes with slower inference and higher cost.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Choosing the largest available embedding model by default is not automatically the right call. A smaller model that runs faster and cheaper often meets a pipeline's actual quality bar just as well.

blocks.text: 6. Multilingual Embedding Models
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447161506-292651246.png
Some embedding models are trained specifically to place equivalent meaning close together across multiple languages.
A query in one language can match a chunk written in another entirely.
7. Benchmarking Embedding Models
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447161506-341255200.png
As covered in more depth under embedding evaluation later in this module, public benchmarks compare models on standardized retrieval tasks.
Those benchmark scores offer a starting point, though testing against real data still matters most.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: A model that ranks highly on a public benchmark does not automatically perform best on a specific pipeline's actual documents and queries. Testing against real data remains the most reliable final check.

blocks.text: 8. Switching Models Cost
As covered in What are Embeddings, embeddings have a fixed length, and two different models produce vectors in incompatible spaces.
Switching embedding models requires re-embedding the entire existing collection from scratch.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing How To Choose An Embedding Model For A New Pipeline

blocks.alt: Recognizing How To Choose An Embedding Model For A New Pipeline
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447161507-100129249.png
Broad, general content suits a general purpose model well.
Narrow, specialized domain content, on the other hand, benefits from a domain specific model.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Choosing the largest available model by default without weighing latency and cost.
Ignoring domain specific models when the pipeline serves a narrow, specialized field.
Trusting public benchmark rankings alone without testing against the pipeline's own real data.
Switching embedding models without accounting for the cost of re-embedding the entire collection.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Embedding models are the actual, trained systems that produce the vectors discussed throughout this module.
Open weight models run locally; hosted API models trade infrastructure control for simplicity.
General purpose models train broadly; domain specific models often outperform them within their niche.
Larger models tend to capture richer meaning, at the cost of slower inference and higher expense.
Multilingual embedding models place equivalent meaning close together across different languages.
Public benchmarks offer a useful starting point, but testing against real data matters most.
Two different models produce incompatible vector spaces, making a model switch costly to execute.
Broad content suits general purpose models; narrow, specialized content suits domain specific models.
